title: JEV 1.14 Integrates Google Harness2 to Boost Vision Benchmark Scores

tickers.name: Alphabet Inc. Class A Common Stock

summary:
The latest deployment of an open-source agent framework has produced accuracy increases across vision-based AI tests without modifying the underlying model weights. Developers integrated Google Research's Harness² into JEV 1.14, allowing the system to autonomously rewrite its own prompts, build tools and distill experience to optimize performance for specific tasks. The team will release a dedicated JEV-Harness² repository soon to share the implementation.

In trials by Google, the framework improved Gemini 3.5 Flash and GLM-5 by as much as 11.8 points on the LAB legal benchmark and 11.5 points on WorkBuddy-Bench by adjusting eight components, including memory and subagents. However, a Google DeepMind paper warns that agents often forget prior knowledge as they adapt to new task streams, since global edits to shared workspaces can overwrite previous experience. The Apache-2.0 licensed project has since reached 11.3K stars on GitHub.

selectedTweets.quotedTweetText:
Google just open-sourced Harness².

(turn any harness into a self-improving system)

a harness is everything wrapped around the model, like the system prompt, tools, memory, skills, and subagents. today a person designs it once, and the agent runs every new task with that same fixed setup.

Harness² lets the agent refine that setup for each new task on its own, with the model weights left untouched.

on every task, the agent proposes edits to its harness, runs a few candidate versions, and composes a better harness by comparing how those runs behaved.

because it learns from the differences between runs, it needs no correct answer or grader for the task.

that covers a single task. Harness² also carries what it learns from one task into the next.

after each task, it saves the harness it settled on along with the lessons that held up across the runs. the next time it refines a harness, it starts from those notes instead of from scratch.

this means every finished task makes the next round of edits more informed.

Google tested this with Gemini 3.5 Flash and GLM-5 on legal, office, and professional work benchmarks. one round of edits was enough to beat their original harnesses, and giving the agent more rounds pushed scores higher.

those extra rounds can go wide or deep. the agent either tries several candidate harnesses at once or keeps refining a single one step by step, using OpenCode or Codex to carry out the work.

you can find the Harness² repo here: https://t.co/i00WLeeFpw

I wrote about a similar idea for agents already running in production, where the harness should repair itself after a failure instead of waiting for someone to debug the trace by hand.

that piece walks through how @Cometml's Opik (open-source) closes this loop, going from a failing trace to a proposed fix to a regression test that stops the same failure from coming back. it's quoted below.

selectedTweets.text:
Can Agents improve their own harness on unseen tasks? The @GoogleResearch team released Harness², a framework that allows improve an harness around a frozen model.

How it works:
1️⃣ Agent runs the base harness on each task to record a baseline trajectory
2️⃣ Editor agent inspects the trajectory, drafts 2 candidate edits (SI, Skills, hooks,….), and runs both.
3️⃣ Composer agent diffs the new trajectory against the baseline, merges edits that fixed failures (within a cap), and runs the final harness.
4️⃣ Reflector agent logs verified lessons into file and saves the winning components to a library for future tasks to pull on demand.

Results:
- 💡 Gemini 3.5 Flash +8.4 on WorkBuddy-Bench and +7.5 on JobBench.
- 🛠️ Skills and scripts drive ~50% of edits; dropping skills costs 5.3 pts.
- 📚 Gemini 3.5 Flash improves on all 3 benchmarks when editing its own harness.

Paper: https://t.co/auogKxwGI0
Code: https://t.co/R4XD6u4M9s

selectedTweets.text:
Google open-sourced Harness². It lets an AI agent improve its own setup on every new task, without retraining the model.

The setup around a model, its "harness", is normally designed once by a person: the system prompt, guardrails, memory, tool guidance, subagents, skills, scripts and plugins. Harness² edits all 8 while it works.

How it works:
→ proposes changes to the harness for the task in front of it
→ tests those changes on that same task
→ keeps what actually worked better, with no answer key needed
→ carries the lessons into future tasks

In Google's tests, one round improved GLM-5 and Gemini 3.5 Flash by up to 11.5 points on WorkBuddy-Bench and 11.8 points on LAB, a legal benchmark.

Works with OpenCode or Codex. The demo runs on Linux with no API keys:
git clone https://t.co/u1Jh52y9oa && cd harness2
uv venv --python 3.12 .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
uv pip install -e '.[render]'
harness2-demo --output runs/demo --k 2

Apache-2.0, 11.3K stars.

selectedTweets.bestBit: more adaptation consistently means agents forget more
selectedTweets.text:
Highly recommended read from Google DeepMind and colleagues.

There is a lot of interest in self-evolving agents, but they're hard to get right.

This work highlights how important and difficult memory and retrieval are in agents.

The big question in this paper is whether self-evolving agents keep learning without forgetting.

They tested ReasoningBank, GEPA, and Meta-Harness on four task streams that drift in topic, workflow, or domain, built from BIRD, BFCL, and ScienceWorld.

The weights stay frozen, and the agents adapt by rewriting prompts, memory, and skills.

Self-evolution improves overall scores on most streams. But more adaptation consistently means agents forget more.

Methods that rewrite a shared prompt or workspace make global edits, so they interfere with unseen tasks and overwrite older knowledge when the stream shifts.

Memory retrieval keeps updates more local, but it still pulls in memories from other domains and collides when similar queries need different workflows.

Static benchmarks hide both problems, so test self-evolving agents on a stream that changes over time.

https://t.co/eO28Lcsj9M
